# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Grassland management at airports is a safety-critical task. Vegetation height and structure on airfield grounds directly influence habitat attractiveness for bird species, which in turn affects the frequency and severity of bird strikes [@devault2011]. At Zurich Airport, grasslands are subject to regular mowing protocols designed to reduce wildlife hazards. However, monitoring when and where mowing occurs has traditionally relied on manual records created by field staff, a process that is labour-intensive and prone to spatial inaccuracies. To investigate the relationship between mowing practices and bird population dynamics, consistent and spatially reliable mowing records are required. 

Satellite-based remote sensing offers a scalable alternative to manual monitoring. The Sentinel-2 constellation, operated by the European Space Agency, provides multispectral imagery at 10 to 20 metre spatial resolution with a revisit cycle of approximately five days [@drusch2012]. Vegetation indices derived from these data, such as the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Normalized Difference Infrared Index (NDII), capture the spectral response of vegetation to management events like mowing, where the abrupt removal of biomass produces a measurable drop in reflectance values [@pettorelli2005; @andreatta2022]. 

In a preceding project work, a pixel-based machine learning workflow for automated mowing detection at Zurich Airport using Sentinel-2 imagery was developed [@klaver2025]. That study demonstrated that standard classifiers, particularly the Support Vector Machine, can detect mowing events with high accuracy on controlled test samples (F1-Score of 0.923). However, the work also identified two fundamental limitations that prevent the system from functioning as a reliable operational tool. 

The first limitation concerns data availability. Optical sensors depend on clear atmospheric conditions, and in the temperate climate of central Switzerland, frequent cloud cover regularly interrupts the temporal chain of observations needed for change detection. This problem is well documented in the literature. De Vroey et al. [-@devroey2021] highlight that relying solely on optical data is particularly problematic in regions where cloud cover is persistent during the growing season. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), which operates independently of weather and illumination conditions, has been proposed as a complementary data source. Several studies have demonstrated that interferometric coherence derived from SAR acquisitions can detect vegetation changes such as mowing, because the removal of biomass alters the scattering properties of the surface [@tamm2016; @zalite2016; @reinermann2022]. 

The second limitation concerns spatial consistency. The pixel-based classification approach produces predictions independently for each pixel, resulting in spatially fragmented output with characteristic salt-and-pepper noise [@blaschke2010]. In the full-scene application conducted in the previous study, models that performed well on test metrics produced scattered false positives across the scene and failed to reconstruct the contiguous shapes of mowing events [@klaver2025]. Spatial postprocessing techniques, such as morphological filtering [@jamil2008] and superpixel-based segmentation [@achanta2012], can address this issue by incorporating neighbourhood context into the classification output. These methods have been applied in remote sensing contexts to improve the spatial coherence of pixel-based classifications [@dharani2021; @crommelinck2017], though their specific application to mowing detection remains underexplored.
  
The main objectives are: 

1. To investigate the integration of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from the Sentinel-1 mission as a complementary input to the existing optical feature set, with the goal of reducing dependence on cloud-free optical acquisitions.
2. To implement and evaluate spatial postprocessing methods that improve the spatial consistency of pixel-based predictions.
3. To benchmark the enhanced workflow against the existing baseline model from the previous study, assessing whether the additions yield measurable improvements in detection robustness and operational reliability.
